Where to stand and when to speak

In training, stand directly behind the shooter, next to the coach, behind the stand or cage and out of any line of the barrels. From there you see what the coach sees, the target and the muzzles together, and the coach can talk to you quietly. Beside the shooter you are close to the swinging gun and the ejected cases, and nobody may be in front of the stand at all.

Choose the mode for the moment. Consecutive interpreting (the coach speaks, pauses, you speak) suits the safety briefing, the walk between stands and the debrief. Whispered interpreting, chuchotage, lets the coach keep talking while you whisper into the shooter’s ear from behind. This works with electronic hearing protection; with passive ear defenders, wait until the gun is open and the shooter can hear you. Whispering is tiring, so alternate the two modes. Agree on a “pause, I’m translating” sign, such as a raised palm.

Timing matters most. The shooter’s routine ends with the shot, and by the time the gun is closed it is well under way. So speak only when the gun is open: between targets, between pairs, after the stand. Between pairs, repeat the coach’s short cues in your language, just as short, such as “more in front”, “head down” or “same again”. Keep the long explanations for later. In training many coaches keep the competition rhythm. At a competition a shooter in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ has at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles. In Compak® Sporting the shooter has at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target. Keep your words short, so the shooter can practise that rhythm.

Tip: Learn the coach’s hand signals at the start and translate them once for your guests. After that they will need you less, and that is a good sign.

Tip: Not sure what the coach said? Ask back with the two options you heard: “Sorry — did you say ‘under it’ or ‘on it’?” It is faster than “Could you repeat that?”

In competition, wait where the squad waits, at the waiting position close to the stand, but out of the shooter’s way. If the referee sees that a shooter was clearly disturbed, the target is a No Bird and is thrown again. Nobody wants to be the cause, so keep silence while anyone is shooting.

Key points

  • Training: directly behind the shooter, next to the coach, out of the barrels’ line
  • Consecutive for briefings and debriefs; chuchotage on the stand; alternate
  • Speak only when the gun is open
  • Training: short cues between pairs, at the competition rhythm (Sporting™ 15 s, Compak® Sporting 10 s)
  • Competition: wait with the squad and keep out of the shooter’s way
Stand Talk

  • Coach Stand right behind me.

    Meaning: Behind the coach and the shooter, out of the swing.

  • Coach Head on the stock — just whisper it to him, I’ll keep going.

    Meaning: Switch to chuchotage and pass the cue on quietly; the coach will not pause. With passive ear defenders, wait until the gun is open.

  • Coach When I do this — hands apart — it means more in front.

    Meaning: The coach explains a hand signal; translate it once for the group.

  • Coach Wait — let him finish the pair.

    Meaning: Hold the advice until the gun is open again.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Where should you stand during a training session on a Sporting™ stand?

    1. Beside the shooter, to see his eyes
    2. Behind the shooter, next to the coach
    3. In front of the cage, facing him
    4. Next to the trap, to watch the target
    Answer

    Behind the shooter, next to the coach

    From behind, out of the barrels’ line, you see what the coach sees and stay safe; beside or in front is dangerous.

  2. What is chuchotage?

    1. Interpreting after the speaker pauses
    2. A written translation of the rules
    3. Translating the coach’s hand signals
    4. Whispering the translation into the ear
    Answer

    Whispering the translation into the ear

    Chuchotage means whispering the translation into the shooter’s ear while the coach keeps talking. Consecutive interpreting is the pause-and-speak mode: the coach says a sentence, pauses, and you translate it.

  3. In Compak® Sporting, how long does a shooter have to call after the previous station’s target was shot?

    1. 10 seconds
    2. 15 seconds
    3. 30 seconds
    4. No limit
    Answer

    10 seconds

    Compak® Sporting gives at most 10 seconds to call; Sporting™ allows at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles.
